applicability: Applies to any finite set of distinct integer nodes (up to 40, magnitude at most 10^6) and integer signs in {-1,0,1} of the same length, with at least one nonzero sign. Returns the smallest positive integer a for which an integer-coefficient polynomial takes values a*signs[i] at nodes[i]. Rejects malformed inputs, duplicate nodes, non-integer values, booleans, and oversized inputs via ValueError. If all signs are zero, returns 1 (the constant zero polynomial works for any a, so the smallest positive a is 1). Limitations: does not handle non-integer nodes or signs outside {-1,0,1}; the polynomial degree is not bounded, but the minimal a depends only on the degree-(n-1) interpolant.
description: The algorithm computes the unique interpolation polynomial Q(x) of degree less than n with Q(nodes[i]) = signs[i] over the rationals, using exact Lagrange interpolation with fractions. It then returns the least common multiple of the denominators of Q's coefficients. This is the minimal positive integer a such that a*Q(x) has integer coefficients. The key theorem: any integer-coefficient polynomial P matching P(nodes[i]) = a*signs[i] can be written as P = a*Q + M*R where R(x)=prod(x-nodes[i]) is monic and M has integer coefficients; conversely if a*Q has integer coefficients then P=a*Q works. Since R is monic, a*Q must have integer coefficients, so the minimal a is exactly the LCM of denominators of Q. Uncertainty: the theorem is standard and exact; the only risk is arithmetic error, mitigated by exact fraction arithmetic.
